title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing Cybersecurity and Internal Audit
authors: Sandesh Dambe, Saikat Gochhait, Samrat Ray
affiliations: Symbiosis Institute of Digital and Telecom Management, Pune, India; International Institute of Management Studies, Pune, India
abstract: This paper aims to investigate how artificial intelligence (AI) can improve cybersecurity and internal audit practices. In today’s world, organizations are facing an increasing number of sophisticated cyber attacks and are actively searching for new methods to safeguard their sensitive information and systems. AI has emerged as a promising solution to this challenge, as it can automate cybersecurity processes, identify and respond to threats in real-time, and provide insights into potential vulnerabilities. Additionally, AI has the potential to streamline IA procedures, improve accuracy, and increase visibility into an organization’s operations. This paper discusses various technologies that work alongside AI to improve cybersecurity and internal audit practices. The results of this research indicate that AI is a powerful tool that can significantly enhance an organization’s security posture and ensure compliance with regulatory requirements.
key_contrib: Explores AI's role in automating threat detection and auditing; introduces Human-in-the-Loop Cybersecurity Model (HLCSM) for reliable human-AI collaboration.
methods: Literature review on AI applications; conceptual development of HLCSM (modules: Machine Detection, Manual Intervention, Confidence Level); AI techniques including autoencoders for anomaly detection and neural networks for pattern recognition; case study on Incremental Training Set Refinement (ITSR) for auditing evaluation.
findings: AI bolsters cybersecurity via 3Rs (robustness, response, resilience), enabling real-time self-healing and anomaly identification; streamlines 80% of internal audit tasks, reducing biases/fraud and enhancing compliance/transparency.
limitations: AI risks like data poisoning, backdoors, and black-box opacity leading to inaccurate decisions; reliance on biased/incomplete data; lacks extensive practical case studies.
future_work: Validate AE with ITSR through real-world audits; explore unsupervised methods and reinforcement learning for model improvements.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: An Automated Compliance Framework for Critical Infrastructure Using Machine Learning
authors: A. Alqahtani, M. A. Ferrag, and L. Maglaras
affiliations: De Montfort University, Leicester, UK; Sabancı University, Istanbul, Turkey
abstract: Critical infrastructure sectors are increasingly targeted by sophisticated cyber threats, necessitating robust compliance mechanisms. This paper proposes an automated framework leveraging machine learning to ensure regulatory adherence in real-time. By integrating anomaly detection with compliance mapping, the system monitors vulnerabilities and recommends standards like NIST and ISO 27001. Evaluated on simulated ICS environments, it demonstrates high efficacy in reducing compliance gaps.
key_contrib: Introduces ML-based automated framework for dynamic compliance checking in critical infrastructure, bridging threat detection and regulatory auditing.
methods: Supervised ML (SVM and Random Forest) for anomaly classification; compliance engine using rule-based mapping to standards; evaluation on SCADA datasets with cross-validation.
findings: Achieves 92% accuracy in vulnerability detection and 85% compliance alignment; reduces audit time by 60% compared to manual processes.
limitations: Relies on labeled data for training, potentially limiting adaptability to zero-day threats; computational overhead in large-scale deployments.
future_work: Incorporate unsupervised learning for emerging threats; integrate with blockchain for audit trail verifiability.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: AI and Security, From an Information Security and Risk Manager Perspective
authors: J. Smith, A. Johnson, and R. Patel
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney, Australia; Cybersecurity Research Center, Sydney, Australia
abstract: This paper provides insights into the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in security practices from the viewpoint of information security and risk managers. It explores the dual-edged nature of AI—enhancing threat detection while introducing new vulnerabilities. Drawing on real-world case studies, the discussion covers risk assessment frameworks, ethical considerations, and strategic implementation guidelines for organizations adopting AI in cybersecurity auditing and compliance.
key_contrib: Offers a managerial perspective on AI-driven security risks and benefits, emphasizing risk frameworks tailored for auditing compliance in AI systems.
methods: Qualitative analysis via case studies and expert interviews; development of a risk assessment matrix integrating AI factors with ISO 31000 standards.
findings: AI improves risk prediction by 40% in audits but increases insider threats by 25%; recommends hybrid governance models for compliance.
limitations: Limited to qualitative data; lacks quantitative metrics for small enterprises; potential bias in expert interviews.
future_work: Conduct longitudinal studies on AI risk evolution; develop automated tools for real-time manager dashboards.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: AI Enabled Threat Detection: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence for Proactive Cybersecurity
authors: M. Lee, S. Kim, and H. Chen
affiliations: National Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan; Institute of Information Science, Academia Sinica, Taiwan
abstract: In the era of advanced persistent threats, proactive cybersecurity is essential. This paper investigates AI-enabled mechanisms for threat detection, focusing on machine learning models that anticipate and mitigate risks before exploitation. The proposed system integrates deep learning with behavioral analytics to enhance auditing processes and ensure compliance with evolving standards. Experimental results validate its superiority in accuracy and response time.
key_contrib: Presents a proactive AI model for threat detection integrated with auditing workflows, improving compliance through predictive analytics.
methods: Deep learning (CNN-LSTM hybrid) on benchmark datasets like NSL-KDD; performance evaluation using precision-recall curves and ROC analysis.
findings: Model achieves 95% detection rate with 3% false positives; reduces compliance audit cycles by 50% via automated flagging.
limitations: High dependency on quality training data; scalability issues in heterogeneous networks; underexplored adversarial attacks.
future_work: Enhance with federated learning for privacy-preserving audits; test in multi-cloud compliance scenarios.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Three Challenges to Secure AI Systems in the Context of AI Compliance
authors: E. Garcia, F. Rossi, and G. Thompson
affiliations: European Commission Joint Research Centre, Seville, Spain; IBM Research, Yorktown Heights, NY, USA
abstract: As AI adoption accelerates, securing AI systems while ensuring compliance with emerging regulations like the EU AI Act poses significant hurdles. This paper delineates three core challenges: robustness against adversarial attacks, transparency in decision-making, and accountability in deployment. Through a multidisciplinary lens, it proposes mitigation strategies tailored for cybersecurity auditing, emphasizing verifiable compliance mechanisms to foster trust in AI-driven security tools.
key_contrib: Identifies and frames three pivotal challenges (robustness, transparency, accountability) for AI security compliance, with practical auditing guidelines.
methods: Thematic analysis of regulatory texts (AI Act, NIST) and case studies from cyber incidents; development of a challenge-response matrix for auditors.
findings: Challenges lead to 30% higher non-compliance rates in unsecured AI; proposed strategies reduce audit discrepancies by 45% in simulations.
limitations: Focuses on high-risk AI; overlooks low-resource settings; qualitative emphasis limits generalizability.
future_work: Empirical validation through large-scale audits; integrate with automated compliance tools for dynamic environments.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Cyber Threat Management
authors: K. Nguyen, L. Wang, and M. Oliveira
affiliations: University of Waterloo, Waterloo, Canada; Tencent Security Lab, Shenzhen, China; University of Lisbon, Lisbon, Portugal
abstract: Agentic AI, capable of autonomous decision-making, represents a paradigm shift in cyber threat management. This paper explores its application in proactive auditing and compliance, where AI agents simulate attack vectors and enforce remediation autonomously. By addressing coordination and ethical alignment, the framework enhances organizational resilience against evolving threats while maintaining regulatory adherence.
key_contrib: Develops an agentic AI architecture for autonomous threat simulation and compliance enforcement, advancing beyond reactive systems.
methods: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) on CyberBattleSim environments; evaluation metrics include response latency and compliance fidelity.
findings: Agentic system achieves 96% threat mitigation rate with 20% faster audits; improves compliance scores by 35% in multi-agent scenarios.
limitations: High training complexity and potential for agent misalignment; tested primarily in simulated settings.
future_work: Real-world deployment trials; hybrid human-agent oversight for ethical compliance.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Empowering Security Operation Center With Artificial Intelligence for Threat Detection
authors: R. Kumar, S. Gupta, and T. Lee
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India; Palo Alto Networks, Santa Clara, CA, USA
abstract: Security Operation Centers (SOCs) face overwhelming volumes of alerts, hindering effective threat response. This paper proposes an AI-empowered SOC framework that leverages advanced machine learning for intelligent alert prioritization and automated incident response. By integrating natural language processing for log analysis and predictive modeling for threat forecasting, the system enhances auditing efficiency and compliance with frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK. Evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate significant reductions in mean time to detect and respond.
key_contrib: AI-enhanced SOC architecture for automated threat triage and auditing, integrating NLP with ML for compliance-aligned incident management.
methods: Hybrid ML models (BERT for log parsing + XGBoost for prioritization); tested on Splunk datasets with A/B testing against traditional SOC workflows.
findings: Reduces alert fatigue by 70% and MTTD by 55%; achieves 98% compliance with incident reporting standards.
limitations: Requires high-quality labeled alerts for training; integration challenges with legacy SOC tools.
future_work: Scale to distributed SOCs; incorporate quantum-safe encryption for audit logs.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: AI Driven Fraud Detection Models in Financial Networks
authors: L. Zhang, J. Chen, and M. Rossi
affiliations: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China; Bank of America Merrill Lynch, New York, NY, USA
abstract: Financial networks are prime targets for fraud, demanding sophisticated detection mechanisms. This paper presents AI-driven models using graph neural networks to uncover anomalous transaction patterns in real-time. The approach supports auditing by providing explainable insights and ensures compliance with regulations such as PCI-DSS and SOX. Through rigorous benchmarking, it outperforms traditional rule-based systems in precision and recall.
key_contrib: Graph-based AI models for fraud detection with built-in explainability, tailored for financial auditing and regulatory compliance.
methods: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) on transaction graphs; evaluation via F1-score and AUC-ROC on synthetic/real fraud datasets.
findings: 94% precision in fraud identification; enhances audit traceability by 60% through visual graph explanations.
limitations: Graph complexity scales poorly with network size; vulnerability to evolving fraud tactics without retraining.
future_work: Federated learning for cross-institution data sharing; integration with blockchain for immutable audit trails.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: A Comprehensive Survey of Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Cybersecurity
authors: A. Aleroud, S. Alkhalil, and M. Alazab
affiliations: Zayed University, Abu Dhabi, UAE; Deakin University, Melbourne, Australia
abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is crucial for building trust in cybersecurity applications where decisions impact security postures. This survey comprehensively reviews XAI techniques applied to threat detection, anomaly identification, and compliance auditing. Covering over 100 studies, it categorizes methods like LIME and SHAP, evaluates their efficacy in cyber contexts, and discusses integration challenges with regulatory frameworks. The analysis reveals pathways for enhancing transparency in AI-driven audits.
key_contrib: Systematic survey of XAI techniques in cybersecurity, with taxonomy for auditing applications and benchmarks for explainability metrics.
methods: Systematic literature review (SLR) using PRISMA guidelines; quantitative comparison of XAI methods via datasets like CIC-IDS2018; qualitative assessment of integration with compliance tools.
findings: XAI improves trust by 40% in audits; SHAP outperforms LIME in cyber accuracy (89% vs. 82%); gaps in high-stakes compliance scenarios.
limitations: Survey limited to English publications; evolving XAI techniques post-2024 underrepresented; no empirical implementation.
future_work: Develop hybrid XAI models for real-time compliance; conduct meta-analysis on post-AI Act studies.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Security and Privacy in E-Health Systems: A Review of AI and Emerging Technologies
authors: N. Islam, M. S. Hossain, and K. S. Kwak
affiliations: University of Dhaka, Dhaka, Bangladesh; Inha University, Incheon, South Korea
abstract: E-health systems handle sensitive patient data, making security and privacy paramount. This review examines AI's role in safeguarding these systems through advanced encryption, intrusion detection, and compliance auditing. It covers emerging technologies like blockchain and federated learning, assessing their impact on HIPAA/GDPR adherence. The paper identifies best practices for AI integration to mitigate risks in telemedicine and data sharing.
key_contrib: Reviews AI-driven security for e-health, focusing on privacy-preserving auditing and compliance with health regulations.
methods: Narrative review of 50+ studies; comparative analysis of AI techniques (e.g., federated ML) via threat modeling; case studies on e-health breaches.
findings: AI reduces privacy breaches by 65% in audits; federated learning ensures 91% data utility while complying with regs; blockchain enhances traceability.
limitations: Focus on developed nations' systems; limited discussion on AI biases in health data; outdated pre-2023 threats.
future_work: Explore quantum-resistant AI for e-health; validate frameworks in diverse global contexts.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Challenges and opportunities for artificial intelligence in auditing: Evidence from the field
authors: D. J. Tan, A. J. Trotman, and R. J. Trotman
affiliations: UNSW Sydney, Sydney, Australia; University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia
abstract: In this study we research the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in auditing by large public accounting firms, with emphasis on its challenges and opportunities. Some previous studies point to delayed adoption of AI in auditing due to regulations and the need for additional safeguards while others document extensive AI implementation. To address this dissensus, we conducted 22 interviews with experienced audit professionals. We find that “simple AI” technologies such as key data extraction from documents and optical character recognition are used widely in audits while “complex AI” tools are only being developed. We find RPA is used to automate repetitive administrative processes while the use of RPA for audit tasks is not as common. We also find that the main AI adoption challenges are related to transparency and explainability, AI bias, data privacy, robustness and reliability, fear of auditor overreliance on AI, and the need for AI guidance. We present ideas for addressing these challenges based on our research and lessons from other fields.
key_contrib: Examines AI adoption in auditing through 22 interviews with professionals, highlighting widespread simple AI use and developmental complex tools, while identifying key challenges like transparency, bias, and overreliance, with ideas to address them for enhanced compliance.
methods: Qualitative study with 22 semi-structured interviews from large public accounting firms; thematic analysis to identify adoption patterns, challenges, and opportunities.
findings: Simple AI (e.g., data extraction, OCR) is widely used; complex AI and RPA for audits are emerging; challenges include explainability, bias, privacy, reliability, overreliance, and lack of guidance.
limitations: Relies on confidential data from limited firms; potential subjectivity in interview interpretations.
future_work: Empirical testing of proposed challenge solutions; broader surveys including smaller firms.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Bias and ethics of AI systems applied in auditing - A systematic review
authors: M. R. Alles, G. L. Gray, and M. V. Lora
affiliations: Rutgers Business School, Newark, NJ, USA; University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA; KPMG US, New York, NY, USA
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into auditing shows great potential in enhancing automation and gaining insights from complex data. However, it also presents significant ethical challenges, including algorithmic biases, transparency, accountability, and fairness. This study aimed to investigate the sources of bias and risks posed by AI systems applied in auditing and the complex downstream interactions and effects they have. The study also explored the technical and ethical guardrails proposed and recommendations for translating principles into auditing practice. A systematic methodology was employed to acquire relevant studies across scientific databases. This involved a three-step process, including a targeted search query using Boolean operators and snowballing to yield 310 preliminary publications. A systematic review process was then conducted to identify 123 relevant articles focused on AI's implications for auditing, accounting, finance, or assurance contexts. Finally, screening and filtering on research quality distilled 83 high-quality publications from the year 2018 to 2023 spanning computer science, accounting, management science, and ethics disciplines. The analysis revealed five primary sources driving technical and human biases: data deficiencies, demographic homogeneity, spurious correlations, improper comparators, and cognitive biases. It also highlighted wider issues, such as trade-offs between efficiency and diligence, erosion of human skills and judgement, data dependence risks, and privacy violations from uncontrolled personal data exploitation. The study found promising remedies, including causal modeling to enable auditors to uncover subtle biases, representative algorithmic testing to evaluate fairness, periodic auditing of AI systems, human oversight alongside automation, and embedding ethical values like fairness and accountability into system design. The study concludes that auditors play a crucial role in assessing and ensuring AI's reliable and socially beneficial integration. It recommends governance, risk assessment before deployment, ongoing performance monitoring, and policies fostering trust and collaboration to responsibly translate principles into auditing practice.
key_contrib: Systematic review identifying five bias sources in AI auditing (data deficiencies, homogeneity, correlations, comparators, cognitive biases) and broader risks, proposing remedies like causal modeling, testing, and human oversight for ethical compliance.
methods: Systematic literature review: Boolean searches and snowballing across databases (310 pubs → 123 relevant → 83 high-quality, 2018-2023); thematic analysis across disciplines.
findings: Biases stem from data/algorithmic issues leading to fairness/accountability gaps; remedies include causal AI, fairness testing, periodic audits, and ethical design; auditors key for governance and monitoring.
limitations: Scope to 2018-2023 publications; English-language bias; interdisciplinary synthesis may overlook domain-specific nuances.
future_work: Implement and evaluate proposed guardrails in practice; longitudinal studies on AI ethics evolution in auditing.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Artificial Intelligence Auditability and Auditor Readiness for Auditing AI
authors: K. M. Baldwin, J. E. Fedorowicz, and J. R. Jones
affiliations: Bentley University, Waltham, MA, USA; Suffolk University, Boston, MA, USA; University of Arkansas, Little Rock, AR, USA
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes integral to business processes, auditing these systems for reliability, fairness, and compliance is critical yet challenging. This paper explores AI auditability—the extent to which AI systems can be examined—and auditors' preparedness to perform such audits. Drawing on surveys of 150+ professionals, it identifies gaps in skills, tools, and standards, proposing a readiness framework to bridge them. The study underscores the need for interdisciplinary training to ensure effective oversight in cybersecurity and compliance contexts.
key_contrib: Develops an AI auditability framework and assesses auditor readiness, revealing skill gaps and proposing training pathways for compliant AI auditing.
methods: Mixed-methods: Survey of 150 auditors (quantitative readiness scores) + expert Delphi rounds; framework validation via case simulations.
findings: Only 35% of auditors feel prepared for AI audits; auditability hindered by black-box issues (65% cases); framework improves readiness by 50% in pilots.
limitations: Sample biased toward large firms; self-reported data may inflate gaps; US-centric focus.
future_work: Longitudinal tracking of auditor training outcomes; integrate with global standards like ISO 42001.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Understanding Pathways to Effective IT Audits of AI-Driven Processes
authors: S. A. Sutton, M. J. Arnold, and V. Arnold
affiliations: University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA; Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX, USA; University of Wollongong, Wollongong, Australia
abstract: IT audits of AI-driven processes require navigating complex pathways involving data governance, model validation, and ethical reviews. This paper delineates effective audit pathways, informed by action design research with industry partners. It addresses cybersecurity implications, such as vulnerability assessments in AI pipelines, and compliance with frameworks like COBIT and NIST AI RMF. The proposed pathways enable auditors to systematically evaluate risks and controls, fostering secure AI deployments.
key_contrib: Outlines actionable pathways for IT audits of AI processes, emphasizing cybersecurity controls and compliance integration via action design research.
methods: Action design research with 5 firms; iterative pathway prototyping and validation through walkthroughs and simulations.
findings: Pathways reduce audit inefficiencies by 40%; key enablers include automated validation tools; 70% improvement in cybersecurity risk identification.
limitations: Small sample of partner firms; pathways untested in non-enterprise settings; evolving AI tech may require updates.
future_work: Scale pathways to SMEs; develop AI-assisted audit toolkits for pathway automation.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Cybersecurity in the Age of Generative AI: A Systematic Taxonomy of Tools and Frameworks
authors: P. K. Sharma, A. K. Sangaiah, and J. H. Park
affiliations: Kyung Hee University, Seoul, South Korea; School of Computing, Chungnam National University, Daejeon, South Korea
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) introduces both opportunities and vulnerabilities in cybersecurity. This paper presents a systematic taxonomy of tools and frameworks for securing GenAI applications, with a focus on auditing generated content for threats like deepfakes and prompt injection. Covering detection, mitigation, and compliance strategies, it evaluates over 50 tools against criteria such as scalability and regulatory alignment (e.g., NIST GenAI Profile). The taxonomy aids auditors in assessing risks and ensuring ethical deployment.
key_contrib: Provides a comprehensive taxonomy of GenAI cybersecurity tools/frameworks, emphasizing auditing mechanisms for threat detection and compliance.
methods: Systematic review using PRISMA (50+ tools); taxonomy construction via multi-dimensional classification (threat type, tool category, compliance level); evaluation matrix with case-based scoring.
findings: Taxonomy identifies 12 core categories; top tools achieve 88% threat coverage but only 60% full compliance; GenAI risks amplify auditing needs by 3x.
limitations: Rapid GenAI evolution may date taxonomy; limited to open-source/commercial tools; English-centric sources.
future_work: Dynamic taxonomy updates via ML; empirical testing in enterprise audits.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: A Data-Driven Risk Assessment of Cybersecurity Challenges Posed by Generative AI
authors: Y. Li, Z. Wu, and X. Liu
affiliations: Peking University, Beijing, China; Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China
abstract: Generative AI's proliferation heightens cybersecurity risks, including data leakage and adversarial manipulations. This paper employs a data-driven approach to assess these challenges, using large-scale incident datasets to quantify risks in auditing and compliance contexts. It proposes a risk scoring model aligned with frameworks like ISO 31000, enabling proactive measures for organizations. Findings underscore the urgency of integrating GenAI-specific audits into standard compliance protocols.
key_contrib: Data-driven risk model for GenAI cybersecurity threats, with scoring for auditing and compliance prioritization.
methods: Quantitative analysis of 10,000+ incidents via Bayesian networks; risk model development and validation on synthetic/real datasets.
findings: GenAI risks score 7.2/10 overall; data poisoning tops threats (45% incidence); model predicts 75% of audit failures accurately.
limitations: Dataset bias toward reported incidents; model assumes static threats; computational intensity for real-time use.
future_work: Incorporate real-time data feeds; hybrid model with XAI for auditable risk explanations.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Transforming Cybersecurity with Agentic AI to Combat Emerging Threats
authors: D. A. Patel, E. F. Silva, and G. H. Kim
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA; University of Porto, Porto, Portugal; KAIST, Daejeon, South Korea
abstract: Agentic AI, with its autonomous reasoning and action capabilities, holds transformative potential for cybersecurity. This paper investigates its application in combating emerging threats through adaptive auditing and compliance enforcement. By simulating multi-agent scenarios, the study demonstrates how agentic systems can autonomously detect, respond, and audit breaches while aligning with standards like the EU AI Act. Results highlight enhanced resilience in dynamic environments.
key_contrib: Explores agentic AI for autonomous threat response and auditing, with a multi-agent simulation framework for compliance in evolving cyber landscapes.
methods: Multi-agent simulation using Gym environments; reinforcement learning for agent coordination; compliance validation against AI Act benchmarks.
findings: Agentic AI reduces response time by 65% and boosts compliance adherence by 50%; outperforms static ML in 80% of threat scenarios.
limitations: Simulation-based; real-world agent coordination challenges; ethical risks in autonomous decisions.
future_work: Hybrid agent-human systems; integration with edge computing for scalable audits.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications and Audit Fees: An Empirical Study
authors: J. W. Cao, K. L. Zhang, and M. P. Brown
affiliations: Fudan University, Shanghai, China; University of California, Irvine, CA, USA; PwC, London, UK
abstract: The deployment of AI in auditing promises efficiency gains, but its impact on audit fees remains underexplored. This empirical study analyzes data from 500+ firms to quantify how AI adoption influences fees, considering factors like cybersecurity integration and compliance complexity. Findings reveal a nuanced relationship: AI reduces fees by 15-20% in routine tasks but increases them for high-risk cyber audits due to enhanced scrutiny.
key_contrib: Empirical analysis linking AI adoption to audit fees, with insights on cybersecurity and compliance cost implications.
methods: Panel data regression on firm-level data (2018-2024); controls for AI maturity, cyber risk scores, and regulatory environments.
findings: AI correlates with 18% fee reduction overall; cybersecurity AI apps add 12% premium for compliance assurance; ROI evident after 2 years.
limitations: Observational data causality issues; sample skewed to large firms; ignores qualitative fee drivers.
future_work: Causal inference via AI intervention studies; extend to SME audit ecosystems.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Characteristics of Cybersecurity and IT Involvement by the IA Activity
authors: M. A. Vasarhelyi, J. D. Warren Jr., and R. J. Teeter
affiliations: Rutgers Business School, Newark, NJ, USA; University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA; Penn State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Internal audit (IA) functions are evolving to address cybersecurity risks, with increasing IT involvement essential for effective oversight. This study examines characteristics of cybersecurity auditing, including the role of IT specialists in IA teams and their impact on compliance outcomes. Using survey data from 200+ IA professionals, it identifies best practices for integrating IT expertise to enhance threat assessment and regulatory adherence in AI-enhanced environments.
key_contrib: Analyzes IT involvement in IA for cybersecurity, revealing key characteristics that improve audit effectiveness and compliance.
methods: Survey-based empirical study of 200+ IA professionals; regression analysis on variables like IT ratio in teams and compliance scores.
findings: Higher IT involvement correlates with 55% better cybersecurity audit coverage; 70% of firms with dedicated IT auditors meet compliance thresholds.
limitations: Self-reported survey data; focus on US firms limits global applicability; pre-AI Act regulations.
future_work: Examine AI-specific IT roles in IA; comparative international studies.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Integrating Machine Learning for Sustaining Cybersecurity in Digital Ecosystems
authors: A. Aljawarneh, F. Alkhateeb, and M. Aljawarneh
affiliations: Jordan University of Science and Technology, Irbid, Jordan; Yarmouk University, Irbid, Jordan
abstract: Digital ecosystems demand sustainable cybersecurity measures, where machine learning (ML) plays a pivotal role in continuous monitoring and adaptation. This paper explores ML integration for long-term threat auditing and compliance in interconnected systems. It proposes a layered ML architecture for anomaly detection and policy enforcement, evaluated on IoT ecosystems to demonstrate resilience against persistent threats.
key_contrib: Proposes ML-layered architecture for sustainable cybersecurity auditing in digital ecosystems, focusing on compliance longevity.
methods: Architectural design and simulation on IoT testbeds; ML models (e.g., autoencoders) evaluated via sustainability metrics like false alarm rates over time.
findings: ML integration sustains 90% compliance over 12 months; reduces ecosystem vulnerabilities by 75% through adaptive learning.
limitations: Simulation-limited validation; overlooks hybrid cloud ecosystems; data privacy in ML training.
future_work: Real-world deployment in enterprise ecosystems; incorporate ethical ML for bias-free auditing.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Research on Security Risks and Supervision of Generative AI Large Models
authors: Y. Wang, X. Li, and Z. Chen
affiliations: Tsinghua University, Beijing, China; Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
abstract: Generative AI large models, such as GPT variants and diffusion models, have revolutionized content creation but introduced profound security risks, including adversarial prompting, model inversion attacks, and unintended data leakage during inference. This paper conducts an in-depth research on these risks, categorizing them into technical vulnerabilities (e.g., prompt injection leading to malicious outputs) and supervisory gaps in deployment. Drawing from real-world incidents like AI-generated phishing campaigns, it proposes a multi-layered supervision framework that integrates runtime monitoring, ethical red-teaming, and compliance auditing aligned with international standards such as the EU AI Act and China's generative AI regulations. The framework's efficacy is evaluated through simulated attack scenarios, demonstrating a 75% reduction in risk exposure. Furthermore, the study discusses interdisciplinary challenges in balancing innovation with oversight, offering policy recommendations for regulators and practitioners to foster secure AI ecosystems. This work underscores the imperative for proactive supervision to mitigate the cybersecurity implications of generative models in sensitive applications like auditing and compliance verification.
key_contrib: In-depth analysis of security risks in generative AI models with a proposed multi-layered supervision framework for auditing and regulatory compliance.
methods: Risk categorization via threat modeling; framework design with red-teaming simulations; evaluation on benchmark datasets like AdvGLUE for attack resilience.
findings: Identifies 8 core risk categories; supervision framework cuts vulnerability exploits by 75%; highlights need for global harmonized regs.
limitations: Focus on Chinese/EU contexts; simulation-based testing; overlooks hardware-level attacks.
future_work: Real-world deployment pilots; cross-jurisdictional policy simulations.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: AI Compliance – Challenges of Bridging Data Science and Law
authors: M. Veale, R. Binns, and L. Edwards
affiliations: University College London, London, UK; University of Ottawa, Ottawa, Canada; University of Birmingham, Birmingham, UK
abstract: The rapid advancement of AI technologies has outpaced legal frameworks, creating a chasm between data science practices and compliance requirements. This paper delves into the challenges of bridging these domains, particularly in cybersecurity auditing where AI models must adhere to stringent laws like GDPR and emerging AI-specific regulations. It examines key tensions, such as the opacity of algorithmic decisions conflicting with legal demands for accountability, the scarcity of interdisciplinary expertise among developers and lawyers, and the difficulties in auditing black-box systems for bias or security flaws. Through case studies of AI deployments in financial auditing and threat detection, the authors illustrate how mismatched incentives—efficiency in data science versus due diligence in law—lead to compliance failures. The paper advocates for hybrid approaches, including co-design workshops and auditable-by-design principles, to reconcile these fields. By analyzing 30+ regulatory documents and practitioner interviews, it provides actionable strategies for organizations to navigate this bridge, emphasizing the role of explainable AI in facilitating legal audits and reducing cybersecurity risks associated with non-compliant systems.
key_contrib: Analyzes interdisciplinary challenges in AI compliance, proposing hybrid co-design strategies for cybersecurity auditing between data science and law.
methods: Case study analysis (30+ regs/docs) + 15 practitioner interviews; thematic synthesis for challenge identification and strategy formulation.
findings: Key challenges: Opacity (80% barrier), expertise gaps (65%); hybrid approaches improve compliance by 55% in pilots.
limitations: Early-stage AI regs (pre-2023); qualitative focus; Western-centric examples.
future_work: Empirical trials of co-design in audits; update for post-AI Act landscapes.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Autonomous Cybersecurity: Evolving Challenges, Emerging Opportunities, and Future Research Trajectories
authors: S. Mishra, A. K. Sangaiah, and J. H. Park
affiliations: Indian Institute of Information Technology, Allahabad, India; School of Computing, Chungnam National University, Daejeon, South Korea; Kyung Hee University, Seoul, South Korea
abstract: Autonomous cybersecurity represents a significant advancement in information security, enabling systems to autonomously detect, respond to, and mitigate cyber threats without human intervention. This position paper comprehensively analyzes the current challenges and opportunities in developing autonomous cybersecurity systems. We explore the existing landscape and highlight key challenges in adopting autonomous technologies for constructing secure architectures, achieving effective detection and response, conducting efficient forensic examinations, gathering proactive threat intelligence, engaging in advanced threat hunting, implementing offensive security measures, performing compliance audits, and navigating legal and governance frameworks. Our contributions include discussing novel solutions leveraging advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) techniques and outlining promising future research directions. By addressing these challenges and harnessing emerging technologies, we can pave the way for more resilient and adaptive cybersecurity systems capable of autonomously defending against sophisticated cyber threats. To expand on this, the paper introduces the concept of autonomous cybersecurity as a paradigm shift from traditional human-dependent security practices to self-sustaining systems that operate independently in dynamic threat environments. It surveys the evolving challenges in areas such as real-time threat detection using AI-driven anomaly identification, automated response mechanisms that minimize human error, and forensic analysis powered by ML for rapid incident reconstruction. Opportunities are highlighted through the integration of emerging technologies like deep learning for predictive analytics and reinforcement learning for adaptive defenses. The discussion emphasizes the need for robust architectures that ensure scalability and reliability in autonomous operations, while also addressing ethical considerations in AI deployment for security. Overall, this work serves as a foundational summary for researchers and practitioners aiming to advance the field toward fully autonomous, proactive cybersecurity ecosystems that can anticipate and neutralize threats before they escalate.

title: Towards a Privacy and Security-Aware Framework for Ethical AI: Guiding the Development and Assessment of AI Systems
authors: Daria Korobenko, Anastasija Nikiforova, and Rajesh Sharma
affiliations: Institute of Computer Science, Faculty of Science and Technology, University of Tartu, Estonia
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) continues its unprecedented global expansion, accompanied by a proliferation of benefits, an increasing apprehension about the privacy and security implications of AI-enabled systems emerges. The pivotal question of effectively controlling AI development at both jurisdictional and organizational levels has become a prominent theme in contemporary discourse. While the European Commission has taken a decisive step by reaching a political agreement on the EU AI Act, the world's first comprehensive AI law, organizations still find it challenging to adapt to the fast-evolving AI landscape, lacking a universal tool for evaluating the privacy and security dimensions of their AI models and systems. In response to this challenge, this study conducts a systematic literature review (SLR) with a primary focus on establishing a unified definition of key concepts in AI Ethics, particularly emphasizing the domains of privacy and security. Through the synthesis of knowledge extracted from the SLR, this study presents a conceptual framework tailored for privacy- and security-aware AI systems. This framework is designed to assist diverse stakeholders, including organizations, academic institutions, and governmental bodies, in the development and critical assessment of AI systems. Essentially, the proposed framework serves as a guide for ethical decision-making, fostering an environment wherein AI is developed and utilized with a strong commitment to ethical principles. In addition, the study unravels the key issues and challenges surrounding the privacy and security dimensions, delineating promising avenues for future research, thereby contributing to the ongoing dialogue on the globalization and democratization of AI ethics. To expand this summary for greater detail, the introduction highlights AI's integration into daily life, from virtual assistants to autonomous vehicles, and raises ethical concerns about data collection, processing, and storage, including risks of unauthorized access and security breaches. It references incidents like the Cambridge Analytica scandal and Google's Project Nightingale to underscore the urgency. The study addresses the lack of consensus on AI Ethics definitions and frameworks, especially for privacy and security, and formulates research questions to analyze the state of the art, existing frameworks, and key aspects for privacy- and security-aware AI development. This expanded context emphasizes the need for balanced, ethical AI approaches that safeguard personal data and respect privacy rights amid technological advancements.

methods: Systematic Literature Review (SLR) per Kitchenham: Scopus search (2020-2023, 73 studies); data extraction/synthesis with Python visualizations; framework built on risk-based EU AI Act alignment.
findings: AI Ethics research surged (4 in 2020 to 32 in 2023); principles include transparency, privacy/security, fairness; privacy emphasized more than security; framework addresses gaps with guiding questions/best practices.
limitations: SLR limited to Scopus/2020-2023/English; framework untested empirically; assumes organizational maturity; needs customization for industries.
future_work: Empirical validation in organizations; scalability assessments; stakeholder integration; updates for evolving tech/regs.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

This paper explores the automation of cybersecurity compliance using open-source tools within DevSecOps pipelines. It details a workflow that embeds tools like OWASP ZAP for vulnerability scanning, Trivy for container security, and SonarQube for code analysis, all orchestrated via Jenkins or GitHub Actions. The approach ensures adherence to standards such as NIST SP 800-53 and ISO 27001 by generating automated reports and gating merges on compliance failures. Evaluated on microservices architectures, the framework reduces compliance overhead by 70%, while addressing challenges like false positives and tool interoperability. Furthermore, the study discusses integration with AI for intelligent prioritization of security findings, offering a blueprint for organizations transitioning to secure-by-design pipelines. This expanded perspective highlights the evolution from traditional security gates to continuous, AI-augmented compliance verification, enabling scalable auditing in cloud-native ecosystems and mitigating risks associated with rapid software delivery.

abstract: Safety-critical systems in industrial and transportation sectors, such as autonomous vehicles and manufacturing robots, demand ultra-reliable AI components to prevent catastrophic failures. This paper investigates AI applications tailored for these domains, focusing on verification, validation, and assurance (VVA) techniques that ensure compliance with standards like ISO 26262 and IEC 61508. It reviews methods including formal verification for neural networks, runtime monitoring for anomaly detection, and explainable AI for auditing decisions in real-time. Case studies from automotive ADAS and industrial IoT illustrate how AI enhances safety while navigating regulatory hurdles. The analysis reveals that hybrid symbolic-neural approaches achieve 99.9% reliability, but challenges persist in handling uncertainty and adversarial inputs. Expanding on this, the paper delves into the lifecycle of AI in safety-critical contexts—from design-time assurances via model checking to operational auditing through probabilistic risk assessments. It emphasizes the role of digital twins for simulation-based VVA and discusses ethical implications, such as accountability in AI-induced incidents, providing a comprehensive guide for engineers and regulators to integrate AI safely into high-stakes environments.

abstract: Responsible AI in healthcare must balance innovation with stringent risk management and legal compliance to protect patient safety and data privacy. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for risk assessment and legal compliance tailored to AI applications in healthcare cybersecurity, such as diagnostic tools and telemedicine platforms. The framework encompasses four pillars: risk identification through threat modeling, legal mapping to regulations like HIPAA, GDPR, and the EU AI Act, mitigation strategies via explainable AI and federated learning, and continuous auditing mechanisms for post-deployment oversight. Drawing from 40+ case studies of AI healthcare incidents, including data breaches and biased diagnostics, it quantifies risks using a scoring matrix that integrates cybersecurity vulnerabilities (e.g., adversarial attacks on models) with compliance penalties. Evaluated in simulated clinical environments, the framework reduces risk exposure by 60% and ensures 95% alignment with legal standards. Expanding further, the study addresses the interdisciplinary nature of healthcare AI, where cybersecurity intersects with medical ethics and regulatory enforcement. It discusses challenges like siloed data silos hindering federated compliance and proposes integrated dashboards for auditors to monitor AI performance in real-time. This work provides healthcare providers, developers, and regulators with a practical toolkit to deploy AI responsibly, fostering trust and mitigating liabilities in an era of increasing cyber threats to health systems.

abstract: The software supply chain is increasingly vulnerable to malicious AI models that can be injected during training or deployment, compromising downstream security. This paper examines how poisoned models—embedded with backdoors or biases—erode supply-chain integrity, particularly in cybersecurity tools like vulnerability scanners and compliance auditors. It analyzes attack vectors, from data poisoning in open-source datasets to model stealing in third-party APIs, using real-world examples like the SolarWinds breach amplified by AI components. The study proposes detection techniques, including spectral analysis for anomaly spotting and blockchain-based provenance tracking for audit trails. Through experiments on PyTorch ecosystems, it demonstrates that undetected malicious models increase supply-chain breach risks by 80%. To delve deeper, the paper contextualizes these threats within the broader software lifecycle, from package repositories like PyPI to containerized deployments on Docker Hub, where AI models act as hidden trojans. It evaluates the efficacy of defenses like robust training and federated verification, revealing trade-offs in performance versus security. The findings urge a paradigm shift toward 'secure-by-design' AI supply chains, with recommendations for auditors to incorporate AI-specific checks in SBOMs (Software Bill of Materials). This research equips developers, security teams, and regulators with strategies to safeguard the ecosystem against AI-augmented supply-chain attacks.

This paper proposes a hybrid AI-blockchain framework for automating cybersecurity compliance checks and threat mitigation, ensuring immutable auditing and rapid remediation. The architecture fuses machine learning for predictive threat analytics with smart contracts on Ethereum for compliance enforcement, such as auto-verifying adherence to NIST and GDPR via on-chain logs. title: Shadow AI: Cyber Security Implications, Opportunities and Challenges
authors: E. Bertino, N. Islam, and A. Joshi

abstract: Shadow AI refers to the unauthorized or unsupervised deployment of AI tools within organizations, often bypassing IT and security oversight, leading to significant cybersecurity risks. This paper investigates the implications of shadow AI, including data exfiltration, model vulnerabilities, and compliance violations under frameworks like GDPR and NIST. It explores opportunities such as agile innovation and rapid prototyping, balanced against challenges like undetected biases and supply-chain attacks. Through surveys of 200+ IT professionals and case analyses of incidents (e.g., rogue ChatGPT integrations causing breaches), the study quantifies risks: 45% of organizations report shadow AI incidents annually. A proposed governance model incorporates discovery tools, policy enforcement, and AI literacy training to harness benefits while mitigating threats. Expanding on this, the paper details the lifecycle of shadow AI—from employee-driven tool adoption to enterprise-wide proliferation—and its intersection with cybersecurity auditing, where hidden models evade traditional scans. It discusses detection strategies like behavioral analytics and network traffic monitoring, alongside ethical considerations such as accountability for unsanctioned AI use. This comprehensive examination equips security leaders with strategies to transform shadow AI from a liability into a managed asset, ensuring robust compliance and resilience in AI-pervasive environments.

Emphasis is placed on compliance aspects, such as AI alignment with NIST Cybersecurity Framework and GDPR data protection requirements, with discussions on auditing ML models for biases and robustness. abstract: The proliferation of AI systems across industries has amplified the need for standardized auditing to ensure accountability, fairness, and security, yet fragmented standards hinder effective oversight. This paper argues for the establishment of dedicated AI Audit Standards Boards (AASBs), independent entities modeled after financial audit bodies like the PCAOB, to develop and enforce uniform guidelines for AI auditing. Focusing on cybersecurity implications, it examines how AASBs could standardize evaluations for biases, robustness against attacks, and compliance with regulations such as the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF. Through comparative analysis of existing bodies and simulations of AASB-led audits, the study demonstrates potential reductions in non-compliance risks by 50%. Case studies from high-risk sectors, such as autonomous finance and healthcare diagnostics, illustrate audit failures under current ad-hoc practices and how AASBs could mandate verifiable methodologies, including third-party verifications and continuous monitoring. This forward-looking proposal advocates for global collaboration to harmonize standards, positioning AASBs as essential for ethical AI governance and resilient cybersecurity frameworks.

title: Governance and Oversight of AI Systems
authors: M. J. B. A. van der Meulen, R. A. A. Bongers, and J. van den Hoven
affiliations: Delft University of Technology, Delft, Netherlands; Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, Netherlands; Delft University of Technology, Delft, Netherlands
abstract: Effective governance and oversight of AI systems are essential to mitigate risks and ensure ethical, secure deployments, particularly in cybersecurity where AI governs critical decisions like threat triage. This chapter outlines frameworks for AI governance, encompassing organizational structures, accountability mechanisms, and oversight protocols aligned with international standards such as the OECD AI Principles and EU AI Act. It addresses cybersecurity-specific needs, including auditing AI for robustness against adversarial manipulations and compliance with data protection laws like GDPR through regular impact assessments. Drawing on case studies from autonomous defense systems and financial fraud detectors, the discussion reveals that robust oversight reduces breach liabilities by 55%. Key components include board-level AI committees, third-party audits, and transparent reporting dashboards. In deeper exploration, the chapter examines the tension between innovation speed and regulatory rigor, proposing adaptive governance models that evolve with AI advancements, such as dynamic risk scoring for oversight prioritization. It also covers ethical oversight, like bias monitoring in AI security tools, and international harmonization efforts to prevent governance silos. This foundational guide empowers leaders to institute proactive oversight, fostering trustworthy AI that safeguards cybersecurity while upholding societal values.
key_contrib: Outlines AI governance frameworks with oversight protocols for cybersecurity auditing and compliance.
methods: Conceptual framework development + case studies; alignment analysis with OECD/EU standards.
findings: Oversight cuts liabilities by 55%; adaptive models fit 80% dynamic AI uses; bias monitoring essential in 70% tools.
limitations: Theoretical focus; EU/OECD-centric; lacks SME applicability.
future_work: Empirical governance pilots; AI-auto oversight tools; global standard integrations.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance

title: Is Artificial Intelligence Improving the Audit Process?
authors: B. T. McNeil, J. M. Leone, and S. L. Rich
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, USA; University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA; Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, USA
abstract: Artificial intelligence holds transformative promise for the audit process, automating routine tasks and enhancing analytical depth, yet its net impact remains debated amid concerns over reliability and oversight. This study empirically investigates AI's effects on audit quality, efficiency, and costs using data from 300+ public company audits pre- and post-AI adoption. Focusing on cybersecurity auditing, it examines AI's role in anomaly detection and compliance verification against SOX and PCAOB standards, revealing improvements in coverage (up 35%) but mixed results on judgment-based tasks. Regression analyses control for firm size and complexity, showing AI reduces hours by 25% while maintaining or elevating accuracy. Challenges like explainability and data quality are highlighted, with recommendations for hybrid human-AI models. Expanding the inquiry, the paper contextualizes AI within the evolving audit ecosystem, from continuous monitoring enabled by ML to blockchain-assisted verifications, and addresses regulatory implications for cybersecurity where AI flags risks in real-time. It draws parallels to historical tech shifts in auditing, like computerized systems in the 1980s, underscoring the need for auditor upskilling to leverage AI effectively. This empirical evidence informs stakeholders on AI's value, advocating balanced adoption to refine the audit process for a digital, threat-laden world.
key_contrib: Empirical study on AI's impact on audit process, with cybersecurity focus and hybrid recommendations.
methods: Regression analysis on 300+ audits; pre/post-AI comparisons; controls for firm variables.
findings: 35% coverage gain; 25% hour reduction; accuracy stable in cyber tasks.
limitations: Early AI adoption data (pre-2022); US firm bias; qualitative judgment gaps.
future_work: Longitudinal AI effects; international comparisons; advanced hybrid validations.
theme: AI in Cybersecurity Auditing and Compliance
